title: How do credit default swaps work?
summary: Josh and Chuck explain credit default swaps (CDS), using a health insurance analogy to illustrate how the instruments work: a buyer pays premiums to a seller who pays out if a debt defaults. They cover the derivative nature of CDS, their origins in the late 1990s on municipal bonds, how they spread to cover any debt, the lack of regulation and the independent arbitration panel, credit event disputes, the role of CDS in the 2007-2008 crisis (Lehman Brothers, AIG bailout), the market's size (roughly $62 trillion in July 2007, reduced to about $20 trillion), and a closing listener mail segment about "Josh and I" versus "Josh and me" grammar.

segments.title: Opening banter and caveat
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with off-topic banter, then Chuck warns that credit default swaps are a difficult topic and Josh will teach him along the way.

segments.title: Health insurance analogy for credit default swaps
segments.summary: Josh explains CDS using an analogy: owning someone else's health insurance policy, and a chain of accidents where no one can pay. He notes health insurance is regulated, while CDS on debt are not.

segments.title: What derivatives are and CDS origins in municipal bonds
segments.summary: CDS are described as derivatives whose value depends on another instrument, compared to oil futures. They began in the late nineties on municipal bonds, which are considered very safe because cities can tax citizens to repay them. Banks earned steady premium income from selling them.

segments.title: Buyers, sellers, and spread to any debt
segments.summary: Josh walks through a buyer who holds city bonds and buys a CDS from a bank. The market grew because no municipalities defaulted, and CDS came to cover any debt. Policies and their sides can be sold to anyone without notice, and there is no regulation.

segments.title: Credit events, disputes, and the arbitration panel
segments.summary: A CDS pays out on a credit event such as bankruptcy or a refusal to repay. Because the market is unregulated, parties can dispute whether an event occurred. An independent arbitration panel of banks, investment houses and investors was formed, with the SEC and Treasury reportedly encouraging it.

segments.title: Market size and the 2007-2008 crisis
segments.summary: The CDS market was valued at about $62 trillion in July 2007, comparable to global GDP of about $69 trillion in 2008. Betting on company failure could pay out more. Lehman Brothers failed as CDS losses cascaded when subprime mortgage securities declined, and AIG received bailout money because of its CDS holdings.

segments.title: Regulation, greed, and the path forward
segments.summary: The market has shrunk to about $20 trillion. Josh and Chuck argue the crisis reflects a pattern of lack of oversight followed by new regulation, and that greed finds loopholes. They conclude that more regulation is likely but that such crises may not be fully prevented.

segments.title: Blog plug
segments.summary: Hosts plug the Stuff You Should Know blog that they write daily, linked from the homepage.

segments.title: Listener mail: I and me grammar
segments.summary: Listener Keith of Alton, Illinois writes that in compound objects like 'send mail to Chuck and I,' either I or me is acceptable, citing Steven Pinker's The Language Instinct. The hosts agree and say they will send Keith a T-shirt. They invite listeners to send grammar feedback by email.
